vignette:
When he speaks about the day his wife was attacked, he does not begin with the phone call. He begins with the weather. It is hot, the kind of late afternoon heat that turns the courthouse steps white and glaring. He is sixty-three then, still working full time as a public defender, carrying two case files under his arm and thinking about what to pick up for dinner on the way home. His wife has gone to the neighborhood market, a routine so ordinary that he barely notices it. The call comes while he is walking to his car. A stranger’s voice says there has been an assault in the parking lot behind the market, that she is being taken to the hospital, that he should come quickly.

He remembers driving but not the route. He remembers the emergency department doors, the smell of antiseptic, and seeing her face swollen in a way that makes his mind reject what his eyes are telling him. She had been struck during a robbery. For several days she remains alive, drifting in and out, and he sits beside her with his suit jacket folded over a plastic chair. He talks to her about mundane things because the truth feels too large to say aloud. He tells her one of his clients finally accepted a plea. He tells her the bougainvillea at home needs trimming. He keeps waiting for the ordinary world to resume. Instead, she dies before the week is over.

In the months afterward, he moves through the funeral rituals with a formal politeness that others mistake for strength. He comes from a family and community where grief is carried with restraint, where dignity is a duty, and he performs that duty carefully. He thanks the relatives who bring food. He bows his head during prayers. He returns to work sooner than anyone advises because he cannot bear the apartment’s silence. At the courthouse, there are calendars, deadlines, clients who need him to be sharp. He tells himself this is mercy.

But the world has changed shape. Parking lots become dangerous terrain. Any sudden call from an unknown number sends a bolt through his chest. He starts scanning every space for exits, for men standing too close, for hands in pockets. When he leaves the office in the evening, he grips his keys between his fingers and circles the block before parking. He tells himself he is being prudent, though the vigilance exhausts him.

Sleep is worse. When he closes his eyes, his mind returns to the hospital, but it also invents what he did not see: her fear in the final seconds at the market, her looking around for help, her calling his name. He wakes soaked in sweat, heart pounding, sometimes halfway out of bed as if he has somewhere urgent to run. On those nights he makes tea at 3 a.m. and sits at the kitchen table staring at the chair she used to occupy. By morning he feels hollowed out, yet he still knots his tie and goes to court.

His work begins to feel altered too. For decades he has believed in procedure, in argument, in the disciplined belief that people are more than the worst thing they have done. After her death, certain cases crack something open in him. If a file mentions assault, he feels his jaw tighten before he has read the second page. In client interviews, he sometimes loses the thread of what is being said because he is suddenly picturing the hospital monitor, the bruising around his wife’s eyes. He grows impatient in ways that shame him. Once, when a young client jokes about a robbery charge, he feels such a surge of rage that he ends the meeting abruptly and locks himself in the restroom until his hands stop shaking.

Outside work, his life narrows. Friends invite him to dinners and community events, but he declines more often than he accepts. The market where his wife was attacked becomes a forbidden place; he drives twenty minutes farther for groceries. He avoids the street entirely if he can. His daughter tells him he is disappearing. He does not argue, because he knows it is true. Even at family gatherings he sits near the door, listening for raised voices, tracking who comes and goes. Celebration feels indecent, as though his attention must remain fixed on the fact of what happened.

He carries guilt with a lawyer’s stubbornness, returning to it as if repetition might produce a different verdict. He thinks he should have insisted she stop going out alone. He thinks he should have answered his phone one minute earlier, should have protected her somehow from an event already over by the time he knew of it. Intellectually, he understands the irrationality. Emotionally, he prosecutes himself without mercy.

Now, five years after her death, he still speaks of her in the present tense before catching himself. He still startles at footsteps behind him. In crowded corridors at court, his shoulders tense and his breath shortens, and for a moment he is no longer an experienced attorney in a dark suit but a husband rushing toward automatic hospital doors. He says the worst part is not only the memory; it is the permanence of being changed by it. The world that once felt difficult but navigable now feels predatory and unstable. He continues to work, to cook simple meals, to call his daughter on Sundays, to water the plants his wife used to tend. From the outside, his life appears intact. Inside it, he lives in ongoing conversation with violence, loss, and the unbearable ordinary afternoon when everything split in two.
